title: Reference Checks and Background Verification: Doing It Right
author: Mawingu HR Solutions
shortDescription: A reference check takes twenty minutes and can save you months of pain. How to verify a candidate properly, lawfully and without wasting the effort.
body:
You have interviewed a promising candidate and you are ready to make an offer. The temptation is to skip the last, unglamorous step — checking references — because you have already made up your mind. Resist it. A short reference check is one of the cheapest forms of insurance a small business can buy against a costly hiring mistake.

Why bother

Interviews reveal how someone presents themselves; references reveal how they actually worked. Verifying employment history and speaking to a past manager confirms that the person is who they say they are, did what they claim, and left on reasonable terms. It is far easier to catch a problem now than to manage it after they have started.

What to verify

  • Employment facts — the roles, dates and responsibilities the candidate stated.
  • Qualifications — where a certificate or licence is genuinely required for the role.
  • Performance and conduct — a former manager's honest view of how they worked and why they left.
A reference check rarely changes a good decision — but every so often it stops a bad one, and that is the whole point.

Ask useful questions

Move past "would you rehire them?" Ask what the person was responsible for, what they did well, where they needed support, and how they handled pressure or conflict. Open questions get you far more than yes/no ones, and a slight hesitation often tells you as much as the words.

Keep it fair and lawful

Get the candidate's consent before contacting referees, and stick to job-related matters. Handle whatever you learn confidentially and use it only to inform the hiring decision. Treat every candidate's information as sensitive personal data — because it is.

Weigh it sensibly

A reference is one input, not a verdict. A single lukewarm comment need not sink a strong candidate, and a glowing reference does not excuse ignoring red flags from the interview. Use references to confirm or question what you already saw — then make a considered decision.
